purpose: One set of minute bars and hand-derived answers, read by BOTH the Python archive rollup (apps/runtime/conversion/candle_rollup.py) and the browser resampler (apps/web/src/lib/chart/resampleBars.ts). Where the two agree the answer is pinned once; where they differ each side's answer is pinned separately with the reason, so a difference cannot change silently in either direction.
oracle: Hand-derived from the minute inputs: open = first minute's open, close = last minute's close, high/low = extremes, volume = sum. Not produced by either implementation.
baseNote: 2026-01-05T00:00:00Z, a UTC day start. Every offset below is in minutes from it.

cases.name: a full hour takes open from the first minute, close from the last and extremes from all
two hours come out in time order even when their minutes arrive in the opposite order
a UTC day from two runs of minutes, complete
a partial hour that starts on the hour: Python publishes it, the browser draws it but marks it still open
cases.difference: Same values. Python has no completeness concept: a published hour is a bar, so a quiet hour is an ordinary bar. The browser flags any hour that is not 60 contiguous closed minutes as closed=false.

cases.name: a sparse hour with holes: Python keeps it, the browser drops it
cases.difference: The archive holds a bar only where the market traded, so Python treats a sparse hour as an ordinary hour. The browser treats a hole between minutes as unknown and refuses to draw an aggregate over it. Open contract question: which meaning does a coarse bar have?

cases.name: an hour whose first minute is missing: Python keeps it, the browser drops it
cases.difference: The browser requires the first minute to sit at the bucket open; Python does not. Same root difference as the sparse hour.

cases.name: a minute belongs to the hour it opens in: 12:59 and 13:00 are different hours
cases.difference: Both sides put the minutes in the same two hours; the browser then drops the first because its lone minute is not at the bucket open, and draws the second as an open hour.

cases.name: a fractional volume: Python refuses, the browser sums floats
cases.difference: Archive volumes are integer contract counts, so Python treats a fractional volume as a defect. The browser also renders spot crypto, whose volumes are fractional, so it sums floats.

cases.name: a price finer than nine decimal places: Python refuses, the browser passes it through
cases.difference: Python converts back to fixed nine-decimal point and refuses anything that would round. The browser holds doubles and never rounds.

cases.name: the same minute delivered twice: Python counts it twice, the browser keeps the last
cases.difference: The browser deduplicates by open time (last wins); Python sums every row it is given. Harmless while published partitions never overlap; a duplicated minute in the archive would double its volume in the hourly rung.
